entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3260"/><div sID="gen4564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3260"/><hi type="bold">7. also by the hand of the prophet Jehu--</hi>This is not another prophecy, but merely an addition by the sacred historian, explanatory of the death of Baasha and the extinction of his family. The doom pronounced against Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.9">1Ki 14:9</reference>), did not entitle him to take the execution of the sentence into his own hands; but from his following the same calf-worship, he had evidently plotted the conspiracy and murder of that king in furtherance of his own ambitious designs; and hence, in his own assassination, he met the just reward of his deeds. The similitude to Jeroboam extends to their deaths as well as their lives--the reign of their sons, and the ruin of their families. <div eID="gen4564" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3263"/><div sID="gen4568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3263"/><hi type="bold">15-18. did Zimri reign seven days--</hi>The news of his conspiracy soon spread, and the army having proclaimed their general, Omri, king, that officer immediately raised the siege at Gibbethon and marched directly against the capital in which the usurper had established himself. Zimri soon saw that he was not in circumstances to hold out against all the forces of the kingdom; so, shutting himself up in the palace, he set it on fire, and, like Sardanapalus, chose to perish himself and reduce all to ruin, rather than that the palace and royal treasures should fall into the hands of his successful rival. The seven days' reign may refer either to the brief duration of his royal authority, or the period in which he enjoyed unmolested tranquillity in the palace. <div eID="gen4568" type="x-p"/>

Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts--</hi>The factions that ensued occasioned a four years' duration (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.15">1Ki 16:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.23">1Ki 16:23</reference>), of anarchy or civil war. Whatever might be the public opinion of Omri's merits a large body of the people disapproved of the mode of his election, and declared for Tibni. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3268"/><div sID="gen4574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3268"/><hi type="bold">24. he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer--</hi>The palace of Tirzah being in ruins, Omri, in selecting the site of his royal residence, was naturally influenced by considerations both of pleasure and advantage. In the center of a wide amphitheatre of mountains, about six miles from Shechem, rises an oblong hill with steep, yet accessible sides, and a long flat top extending east and west, and rising five hundred or six hundred feet above the valley. What Omri in all probability built as a mere palatial residence, became the capital of the kingdom instead of Shechem. It was as though Versailles had taken the place of Paris, or Windsor of London. The choice of Omri was admirable, in selecting a position which combined in a union not elsewhere found in Palestine: strength, beauty, and fertility [Stanley].<div eID="gen4574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">two talents of silver--</hi>£684. Shemer had probably made it a condition of the sale, that the name should be retained. But as city and palace were built there by Omri, it was in accordance with Eastern custom to call it after the founder. The Assyrians did so, and on a tablet dug out of the ruins of Nineveh, an inscription was found relating to Samaria, which is called Beth-khumri--the house of Omri [Layard]. (See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.5">2Ki 17:5</reference>). <div eID="gen4575" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3270"/><div sID="gen4577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3270"/><hi type="bold">29-33. Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all that were before him--</hi>The worship of God by symbols had hitherto been the offensive form of apostasy in Israel, but now gross idolatry is openly patronized by the court. This was done through the influence of Jezebel, Ahab's queen. She was "the daughter of Eth-baal, king of the Zidonians." He was priest of Ashtaroth or Astarte, who, having murdered Philetes, king of Tyre, ascended the throne of that kingdom, being the eighth king since Hiram. Jezebel was the wicked daughter of this regicide and idol priest--and, on her marriage with Ahab, never rested till she had got all the forms of her native Tyrian worship introduced into her adopted country. <div eID="gen4577" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3272"/><div sID="gen4580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3272"/><hi type="bold">34. In his days did Hiel the Beth-elite build Jericho--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Josh.6.26">Jos 6:26</reference>). The curse took effect on the family of this reckless man but whether his oldest son died at the time of laying the foundation, and the youngest at the completion of the work, or whether he lost all his sons in rapid succession, till, at the end of the undertaking, he found himself childless, the poetical form of the ban does not enable us to determine. Some modern commentators think there is no reference either to the natural or violent deaths of Hiel's sons; but that he began in presence of his oldest son, but some unexpected difficulties, losses, or obstacles, delayed the completion till his old age, when the gates were set up in the presence of his youngest son. But the curse was fulfilled more than five hundred years after it was uttered; and from Jericho being inhabited after Joshua's time (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.13">Jud 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">2Sa 10:5</reference>), it has been supposed that the act against which the curse was directed, was an attempt at the restoration of the walls--the very walls which had been miraculously cast down. It seems to have been within the territory of Israel; and the unresisted act of Hiel affords a painful evidence how far the people of Israel had lost all knowledge of, or respect for, the word of God. <chapter eID="1Kgs.16"/>
